title: Auditing AI Decision Models: What We Learned Testing JEV on 1,500+ Leads
excerpt: We ran an empirical black-box audit on TypeSafe AI's JEV across 1,570 leads. Here is why raw AI confidence scores are dangerously misleading—and how a simple 50-sample calibration wrapper fixes them.
author: Athalla Rizky
body:
## The Seduction of the "Confidence Score"

When a machine learning model or an AI decision API returns a decimal like `0.85`, human intuition leaps to a dangerous conclusion: *"This means there is an 85% probability that this event will happen."*

Product teams love this illusion. It feels quantitative, scientific, and clean. We build automated workflow triggers around it:

```typescript
if (lead.score > 0.8) {
  assignDedicatedAccountExecutive(lead)
} else if (lead.score < 0.2) {
  dropFromOutreachQueue(lead)
}
```

There is only one problem: **raw AI confidence scores are rarely true probabilities**. Most neural models and proprietary black boxes output relative logit rankings compressed through activation functions. They are notoriously uncalibrated. A model outputting `0.85` might correspond to an empirical conversion rate of 40%—or 95%—depending on the underlying data distribution.

While developing **Kodeva** (a modern B2B SaaS storefront), we decided to turn the platform into an empirical laboratory to test this firsthand. We integrated **JEV**—a state-of-the-art decision model from TypeSafe AI designed to answer structured evaluation questions—and subjected it to an exhaustive calibration audit on inbound lead scoring.

Here is what we discovered after running 1,570 synthetic leads through the engine across three macroeconomic scenarios.

## The Audit Setup: Owning the Ground Truth

If you ask an AI model to evaluate historical leads, you run into the survivor bias trap: real-world sales teams interfere with outcomes, and uncontacted leads have unknown conversion states.

To audit JEV objectively, we built a **deterministic ground-truth generator** in TypeScript using a seeded PRNG (`Mulberry32`). The generator simulated 1,570 enterprise inquiries across three macroeconomic worlds:

1. **Baseline World (18.1% true conversion):** Standard marketing distribution across Google Search, Instagram, and direct channels.
2. **Drift-Source World (20.4% true conversion):** Inbound traffic shifted toward cold social channels.
3. **Drift-Price World (6.5% true conversion):** Macroeconomic tightening where customer willingness to pay drops sharply.

The generator assigned each synthetic inquiry secret ground-truth parameters (`pTrue` and a Bernoulli outcome). JEV only saw the customer features (traffic source, contact method, form completion speed, landing page) and was asked whether the lead would convert within 30 days.

## Finding 1: Raw Scores are Static and Blind to Drift

The initial findings were startling. JEV did not output genuine probabilities—it output an almost invariant baseline score:

| World Scenario | JEV Mean Score | True Conversion Rate | Expected Calibration Error (ECE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** | `0.419` | **18.1%** | `0.238` |
| **Drift-Source** | `0.414` | **20.4%** | `0.210` |
| **Drift-Price** | `0.418` | **6.5%** | **0.352** |

Notice the pattern? While real-world conversion collapsed from 20.4% down to 6.5%, JEV's average score remained virtually identical at `~0.42`.

In the price-drift scenario, JEV looked at leads that convert only 6.5% of the time and declared a 41.8% conversion likelihood. It was **6.4× overconfident**. The model had no intrinsic mechanism to sense macroeconomic shifts. If we had wired automated sales resources to its raw confidence score, we would have burned outreach budgets chasing leads that had virtually no intent to buy.

## Finding 2: Platt Scaling Fixes Miscalibration for Free

Fortunately, miscalibration is not a fatal defect—provided you recognize it.

We wrapped JEV's raw outputs with **Platt scaling**, a classic statistical technique that fits a two-parameter logistic sigmoid over the model's logit scores:

$$p_{\text{calibrated}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a \cdot \text{logit}(p) + b)}}$$

Applying this post-hoc transformation collapsed the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) from **0.267 down to less than 0.02**.

Even more importantly, we analyzed the out-of-sample learning curve to determine how much historical data was necessary to fit these parameters. The curve flattened completely at **$n \approx 50$ labeled outcomes**.

You do not need thousands of expensive data points or complete model retraining to fix an uncalibrated black box. Tracking just 50 genuine conversion outcomes is enough to calibrate a commercial decision model to your specific domain.

## Finding 3: Margin is an Honest Signal

JEV provides a secondary metric alongside its primary score: a decision margin reflecting how decisively it chose between competing categories.

When we measured the rank correlation between this margin and the model's prediction error ($|p - p_{\text{true}}|$), we found a strong and consistent negative correlation across all three worlds:

$$\rho = -0.43 \text{ to } -0.55$$

In plain English: when JEV reported a high margin, its score was genuinely closer to ground truth. When the margin was narrow, its error rate surged. Unlike the raw probability score, the margin metric was honest out of the box without requiring post-hoc calibration.

## Architectural Takeaways for Production AI

Our journey with JEV crystallized three core architectural rules for integrating AI decision models:

1. **Enforce an Advisory-Only Gate:** Never connect raw AI confidence scores directly to irreversible production triggers. In Kodeva, we display calibrated conversion potential (`pPlatt`) alongside qualitative triage badges (🔴 High / 🟡 Medium / 🟢 Low) in `/admin/leads` to assist human sales representatives, but the system never automates pipeline rejections.
2. **Calibrate Before You Consume:** If an AI vendor claims their API outputs "probabilities," assume they are uncalibrated until proven otherwise. Build an empirical harness and fit a lightweight logistic scaler using your first 50 ground-truth outcomes.
3. **Decouple the Instrument from the Provider:** Wrap third-party models in an interface (like our `JevClient`) and maintain a mock implementation capable of injecting intentional biases. Proving that your testing harness can detect known flaws is the only way to trust its findings on real models.

AI decision models hold enormous promise for business automation. But treating their confidence scores as objective gospel is an operational hazard. With classical statistical calibration and defensive software architecture, you can turn deceptive raw scores into reliable decision instruments.
